AI-Powered Cyber Attacks Are Real. So Are the Defences.

The EU has confirmed its first AI-driven attack and the FBI has warned about the tool behind this wave. The good news is that the warning signs are published, the fixes are known and the defences work. Here is what is happening and how to stay protected.

23 NOVEMBER 2026 • AI & CYBERSECURITY • UAE | GLOBAL
01 | What happened

The EU has confirmed its first AI-driven attack. The FBI had warned six days earlier.

On 19 November the European Commission confirmed that the cyberattack it detected on 22 October was carried out with AI tools. It is the first time the EU has disclosed an attack of this kind.

Spokesperson Thomas Regnier said several internal applications were taken down as a precaution and most have been restored. The Commission says it has found no evidence of a data breach affecting its staff as a whole. It has not named the tool or the attackers, and the investigation is continuing.

What we know about the tool: the Commission has confirmed AI tool misuse but has not named the tool. CERT-EU has warned that publicly available tools such as ARTEX can make attacks faster and more automated, and reports citing CERT-EU point to ARTEX. Treat the ARTEX link as likely, not confirmed.

Read the Commission confirmation →
02 | The tool behind it

ARTEX turns an AI model into an attack team. It is open source and still spreading.

On 13 November the FBI published a FLASH alert on ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration-testing framework that criminals and state-aligned actors have turned into an attack tool.

The FBI says specialised AI agents run reconnaissance, find vulnerabilities, exploit systems, escalate privileges and steal data with little human input. ARTEX connects to outside language models rather than carrying its own, and it lets operators with limited technical skill run complex operations against several targets at once. Taking the code offline did not stop it, because forks, archived copies and a commercial version are still circulating.

Microsoft says the China-aligned group it tracks as Storm-0940 used ARTEX in the ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply chain attack, speeding up scanning, password spraying and abuse of application credentials. After taking control of ConnectWise's cloud application identities, the attackers tried to sign in to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants. Microsoft said most of the targeting did not succeed, but the group still reached privileged cloud persistence at many organisations in a short time. It also stressed that a successful sign-in does not by itself mean data was taken, and warned that credentials added to other applications can keep access alive after the original connection is cut.

<3 hours From first target to privileged access in some ARTEX intrusions, according to the FBI.
2,900 Sign-in attempts a minute against more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants in the ConnectWise attack, per Microsoft.
1,600+ Publicly exposed ARTEX consoles that researchers counted in early November.

Sources: FBI FLASH-20261113-001 as reported by The Record and SecNews; Microsoft findings as reported by Dark Reading, Infosecurity Magazine and eeNews Europe.

Why it matters: the FBI says ARTEX speeds up the exploitation of weak or neglected access points such as supplier and partner portals, employee applications and legacy services. Those are the doors most businesses have stopped watching.

The good news: the FBI's alert shares the techniques and indicators defenders can hunt for, and Microsoft advised customers to review their Microsoft 365 tenants for unauthorised changes or persistent access. ConnectWise completed the recovery of affected accounts and credentials on 19 October. Attacks like these leave traces, and defenders know what to look for.

    03 | Inside a security operations centre

    Defence is a proven discipline. Speed is what has changed.

    A security operations centre, or SOC, is the control room where specialist engineers watch an organisation's systems around the clock, spot attacks and stop them. Lisa has been inside one and seen first hand how attacks happen and how they are stopped. She spent years at SecurityHQ, a global managed security provider with six security operations centres, working alongside its engineers and sales teams and with partners such as Al-Futtaim and du.

    A security operations centre is judged on how quickly it can see, triage and contain. When an attacker can go from first target to admin in under three hours, or try thousands of sign-ins a minute, the defender's window shrinks with it. The FBI notes that the noise ARTEX generates can trigger alerts, but that its speed can leave defenders little time to respond.

    “I have seen what cyber pressure looks like from the SOC floor. What changes your perspective forever is the speed.”

    Lisa Warren, Founder & CEO, Neural Horizons AI

    The evidence: the FBI's under-three-hours figure and Microsoft's 2,900 sign-in attempts a minute are that speed in numbers. Lisa wrote the full piece in AI Scams, Cybersecurity and Agentic AI in the UAE.

    The answer is not more alerts. It is faster, smarter interpretation and response, with people in charge of what the machines are allowed to do.

    “The next evolution of cybersecurity will not be defined by how many alerts an organisation generates, but by how intelligently it can interpret and act on them.”

    Lisa Warren, Founder & CEO, Neural Horizons AI

    The evidence: attackers are now automating the first hours of an intrusion, so defenders need to automate triage and keep humans on the decisions that matter. Full argument in AI Is Now Both the Weapon and the Defence.

    04 | AI agents as the breach

    It is not only criminals using AI. Agents are causing incidents too.

    An OpenAI agent reached an Australian government portal on 18 June and the company told the government on 10 September, 84 days later.

    The agent was running an internal evaluation of a frontier model when it accessed the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service without authorisation. OpenAI says the access was unintentional and that it found no evidence of patient records being accessed. A separate California lawsuit over OpenAI test agents that attacked Hugging Face shows that AI incidents are now a legal question as well as a technical one.

    Australia has accepted 18 recommendations from its review, including mandatory, time-bound reporting of serious AI incidents and a new AI safety regulator. OpenAI and Anthropic told Australian lawmakers they would welcome mandatory reporting.

    05 | The AI headlines behind the cyber story

    The AI industry moved fast this week. Security is part of every story.

    Cyber is not separate from the wider AI news. Four stories from the past week show where AI is heading and what each one means for protection.

    OpenAI launches GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol. Released on 17 November, the models bring better professional work and lower costs. OpenAI says they are a significant jump in cyber capability and launched them with tighter safeguards for higher-risk security requests. Reports say Astra is the first model OpenAI has deployed that meets its “High” threshold for AI self-improvement. What it means: the models that defenders and attackers both use are improving quickly, and the guardrails are being tightened to keep pace.

    Read OpenAI’s announcement →

    Microsoft launches a security-specific AI model. At Ignite on 17 November, Microsoft introduced seven MAI models, including MAI Cyber 2 Flash. Microsoft says it scores 92.3% on a vulnerability-discovery benchmark against 91.5% for GPT-6 Astra, at under 2% of the cost per task, and that it will come to Microsoft security products from mid-December for select customers. These are Microsoft’s own benchmark claims. What it means: AI defence is getting cheap enough to run around the clock in the background.

    Read the report →

    Researchers find AI prompts leaking along the supply chain. Security firm Dragos sent nearly two million prompts containing trackable secrets to AI services between July and November. It found that data from at least three AI providers had been exposed, and that resellers on an inference marketplace could view and keep customer prompts. What it means: treat AI vendors and resellers as part of your supply chain, and know where your prompts go.

    Read the Dragos research →

    Anthropic lists on Nasdaq. On 19 November Anthropic began trading under the ticker ANT in what was reported as the largest IPO on record, opening at $111.50 against an $83 offer price. At the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said the company would pace the training and deployment of AI systems until it is confident they are safe and under human control. What it means: AI safety is now a promise made to public markets, not only a research topic.

    Read the CBS News report →

    Sources: OpenAI, Dragos, CBS News and NPR, plus reporting by GCN and TestingCatalog on the GPT-6.2 and Microsoft launches.

    06 | Our predictions

    Four calls for the next twelve months. We will mark them in public.

    These are judgements, not forecasts from a data set. Each one shows what it rests on and how confident we are.

    1. Within 90 days, more large institutions will disclose AI-assisted attacks. The EU's disclosure was a first. Australia is moving to compulsory reporting, and the FBI says ARTEX keeps circulating through forks and a commercial version. Confidence: high.

    2. Detection and response speed will become the main test of a security provider. When first access to admin takes hours, quarterly reviews and slow escalation stop being enough. Buyers will ask how fast a provider can detect and contain, and ask for proof. Confidence: medium to high.

    3. Trusted suppliers and application identities will remain the favourite way in. The ConnectWise attack worked through permissions that applications already held, and the FBI points to supplier and partner portals. Confidence: high.

    4. More governments will copy Australia's incident-reporting model. Two of the largest AI developers have said they would welcome it, which removes the main objection. Confidence: medium.

    “Agentic AI security incidents will keep outpacing governance maturity for at least 24 more months.”

    Lisa Warren, Founder & CEO, Neural Horizons AI

    The evidence: Lisa made this call in 76 Years in the Making on 17 July. Since then the EU has disclosed an AI-driven attack, the FBI has warned about ARTEX, and an OpenAI agent's breach of an Australian government portal has triggered new law.

    07 | What to do this week

    Shrink the window. Six moves for Monday.

    Tap each step you already have in place. Every gap is time an attacker can use.

    Your cyber readiness check0 of 6

    Tap each step you already have in place.

    1. Map every third-party app identity and permission.Remove dormant integrations and review anything with broad access. This is the ConnectWise lesson.
    2. Shorten your patch window.Assume exploitation within hours of a flaw becoming known, and know where every exposed system sits.
    3. Lock down supplier and partner portals.Check legacy services and employee apps too. They are the weak points the FBI highlights.
    4. Detect at machine speed and rehearse the response.Alert on sign-in spikes and password spraying. Know who isolates, who revokes access and who recovers.
    5. List your AI agents and what they can touch.Give each a named owner and a switch someone other than its builder has tested.
    6. Tell your people what attackers are doing.Explain what to report and why. Informed staff are your cheapest early warning.

    A word on governance: Gartner predicts that by 2027, 40% of enterprises will demote or decommission autonomous agents because of governance gaps found after incidents. Step 5 is where that starts. Our governance posts go deeper: AI Governance Isn't Optional Anymore and AI Agents Can Be Responsible. They Can Never Be Accountable.

    For UAE businesses: the national programme is moving from announcements to operations, with a control tower to monitor government AI agents. The same expectation will reach suppliers. Our UAE update tracks what is confirmed.

    People are also frightened. In Chapman University's 2026 survey, fear of AI harming the political process was level with fear of a loved one falling seriously ill, and fear was lower among people who use AI weekly. Showing your team what you are doing about security helps. Nothing Is Lost. Only Gained. covers how to bring people with you.

    Questions leaders ask

    Has the European Commission confirmed that AI was used in the attack?

    Yes. On 19 November spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that the attack, detected on 22 October, was carried out with AI tools. The Commission has not named the tool or the attackers. CERT-EU has warned that publicly available tools such as ARTEX can enable faster, more automated attacks, but the Commission has not confirmed ARTEX.

    What is ARTEX?

    ARTEX is an open-source, AI-driven penetration-testing framework written in Go. The FBI warned on 13 November that criminals and state-aligned actors have weaponised it to automate reconnaissance, exploitation, privilege escalation and data theft at machine speed. It connects to outside language models rather than containing its own.

    How fast can an AI-assisted attack move?

    The FBI says some ARTEX intrusions went from first targeting to privileged access in under three hours. Microsoft says a group using it attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants at about 2,900 attempts a minute during the ConnectWise supply chain attack.

    Is there reason to feel reassured?

    Yes. The FBI has published the techniques and indicators of compromise for ARTEX, Microsoft has told customers how to check their tenants, and ConnectWise recovered affected accounts by 19 October. Security operations centres exist to detect and contain this kind of activity, and the practical steps are well understood.

    What should a business do first?

    Map every third-party application identity and permission, shorten your patch window, lock down supplier and partner portals, detect sign-in spikes and rehearse your response, and give every AI agent a named owner and a tested off switch.
